name: HiGMem

paper.title: HiGMem: A Hierarchical and LLM-Guided Memory System for Long-Term Conversational Agents

construction.unit: Turn node (raw turn + LLM metadata), grouped under Event nodes
construction.kept_as: verbatim turn text + LLM context sentence, keywords, tags; event summary written by the LLM
construction.processing: LLM annotates each turn; LLM assigns it to one or more of the 10 most similar events or opens a new event; small events get their summary rewritten

organization.structure: two levels: events over turns (a turn may join several events)
organization.stores: turn store + event store (character profiles exist in code but are off in the paper setting)
organization.index: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 dense over turn text (with speaker, date) and over event keywords + tags + summary

management.operations: join existing events or NEW_EVENT; refresh event summary, keywords, tags and facts while the event has < 10 turns, then keywords/tags only

retrieval.query: LLM keyword rewrite of the question for both searches; the original question for the LLM steps
retrieval.candidates: top-10 turns + top-10 events by cosine similarity
retrieval.selection: one LLM call per event picks its turns; the union is filtered by an LLM in chunks of 10
retrieval.budget: no fixed cap; 8.09 turns per question on average (LoCoMo10)

use.context: selected turns with date, speaker, text and the LLM context sentence, sorted by date string
use.reasoning: single answer call with a LoCoMo-category-specific prompt

classify.note: Dense search only proposes candidates; LLM calls pick turns inside events and filter the union, so the LLM fixes the final set.

stages.ingestion: Each LoCoMo turn is added in order, with its speaker and session date.
stages.construction: An LLM writes keywords, tags and a one-sentence context for the turn; the raw text is kept as the Turn node's content.
stages.organization: The turn is embedded, the 10 most similar events are shown to an LLM (by title), and the LLM joins the turn to one or more of them or opens a new event.
stages.update: While an event has fewer than 10 turns the LLM rewrites its 2-3 sentence summary, keywords and tags and appends facts; after that only keywords and tags can change.
stages.retrieval: An LLM rewrites the question as keywords; dense search returns 10 turns and 10 events; an LLM reads each event's summary and turns and picks the useful turns; an LLM filter keeps the relevant ones from the union.
stages.answer: The kept turns (8.09 on average) are given to GPT-4o-mini with date, speaker, text and context sentence, under a category-specific short-answer prompt.

summary: Two-level event-turn memory where event summaries act as anchors: an LLM reads each retrieved event and picks which of its raw turns to pass on, giving a much smaller evidence set than vector top-k.
notes:
Venue: Findings of ACL 2026 per CITATION.bib in the official repo (arXiv v2, 22 Apr 2026). Paper setting in code = --ablation-no-profile --ablation-event-metadata-only --ablation-no-link --k_event 10 (README). Internal code name 'fphm'. Baseline ReadAgent and MemoryBank numbers in Table 1 equal A-Mem's Table 1 (GPT-4o-mini) rounded; the paper does not say they were copied.
DESIGN: §3.1-3.3, §4.1, App. C; code fphm_core.py, run_fphm_evaluation.py at the pinned commit.

sources.code_note: Commit f275072f (2026-04-22, 'Prepare public HiGMem release'), the same day as arXiv v2; the README gives the exact flags for the paper setting. Result logs are not in the repo, so the run behind Table 1 cannot be checked.

headline: The answer model reads raw turns, not summaries: event summaries only steer which turns are picked.
In the paper setting the event fact sheet is written but never read, and turn keywords/tags are never indexed.
Evidence size is set by LLM judgement, not a top-k: 8.09 turns on average versus 99.84 for A-Mem.

open_questions: Table 5 removes the event layer but does not state its turn budget; App. B.1 uses top-100 flat turns. The two ablations give 0.39 and 0.46 F1, so the size of the hierarchy's gain depends on which flat baseline is used.
Adversarial F1 (0.78) comes from a two-way choice prompt; the gain over A-Mem there may reflect answer formatting and a smaller context rather than retrieval.

glance.a: A Turn node: the raw dialogue turn with speaker and date, plus an LLM context sentence, keywords and tags.
The turns are kept verbatim. Events hold a 2-3 sentence LLM summary, which steers retrieval but never reaches the answer model.
Two levels: an LLM joins each new turn to one or more of the 10 most similar events, or opens a new one.
No cross-encoder. GPT-4o-mini picks turns inside each retrieved event and then filters the union, 10 candidates per call.

glance.q: What does the answer model read?
glance.a: About 8 raw turns per question, each with date, speaker and the one-sentence context; no event summaries.

steps.what: turns and events from dense search
shown to one LLM call per event
turns kept by the LLM filter

Small events get their summary rewritten on every join; after 10 turns the summary is frozen and only keywords and tags change.

text: A keyword query retrieves 10 turns and 10 events; an LLM reads each event's summary and turns and picks likely evidence.
An LLM filter then trims the union, so the answer model sees about 8 raw turns instead of a fixed top-k.

rows: flat top-100 turns + same LLM filter (App. B.1)

components.role: Turn annotation, event joining and updates

discussion.takeaway: Let an LLM use short event summaries to decide which raw turns to read. On LoCoMo10 this keeps recall close to A-Mem while passing about 12 times fewer turns to the answer model.

claims.claim: Best F1 on four of five LoCoMo10 categories.
claims.evidence: Multi-hop 0.31, open-domain 0.15, single-hop 0.49, adversarial 0.78; temporal 0.34 is below A-Mem's 0.39. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: A compact, precise evidence set rather than a bigger one.
claims.evidence: Avg K 8.09 vs 99.84, Precision@K 0.1909 vs 0.0101, Recall@K 0.7241 vs 0.7502. Table 2

claims.claim: The event layer matters, not only the LLM filter.
claims.evidence: Without events F1 0.39 / Recall 0.55 (Table 5); flat top-100 + same filter F1 0.46, Precision 0.065, K 22.7 (Tables 6-7)

claims.claim: Cheaper when a small model builds memory and a large model answers.
claims.evidence: GPT-5 answer tokens 25.38M → 1.62M; total $17.43 → $6.43. Table 3, App. B.3

limits: Extra LLM calls for construction and evidence selection; the benefit depends on using a cheap model for memory and an expensive one for answers.
Relies on the LLM judging relevance from event summaries and candidate turns.
On multi-party DialSim it scores lower F1 than A-Mem (0.42 vs 0.49) despite far fewer turns; broader tests on noisy, multi-party conversations are needed.
reading: The paper setting in code annotates each turn in isolation, keeps event summaries only as routing text, and never reads the event fact sheet or turn keywords/tags, so the answer depends on raw turns plus the one-sentence context.

Construction costs more than A-Mem (21.2M vs 9.2M tokens, 15.59 vs 6.38 s per turn), and QA-stage tokens are also higher (29.3M vs 25.5M, Table 9); the saving appears only when the answer model is priced far above the memory model.
Adversarial questions are answered by choosing between the distractor and 'Not mentioned in the conversation', so that category's F1 behaves like a two-way accuracy.
Turn keywords and tags are generated for every turn but never indexed: the turn index text is speaker, date and raw content only.
The final context is sorted by the session date string as text, so turn order is not guaranteed to be chronological.
ReadAgent and MemoryBank rows equal A-Mem's published GPT-4o-mini numbers rounded; Base LLM and A-Mem differ from A-Mem's paper, so they appear to be reruns.

abstract.text: HiGMem targets a trade-off in conversational memory: vector search finds relevant turns but also returns many look-alike turns that inflate the answer context. It stores every dialogue turn with light LLM metadata and groups turns into events that carry a short summary. At question time an LLM reads the retrieved events' summaries and turns, predicts which turns are worth passing on, and filters the result. On LoCoMo10 with GPT-4o-mini it has the best F1 on four of five categories and passes about 8 turns per question instead of about 100.
